newsitem.title: UK: UK MPs demand stronger parliamentary rights from EU.
newsitem.headline: UK MPs demand stronger parliamentary rights from EU.

text.p: The rights of national parliaments within the European Union must be safeguarded, something EU policy falls short of achieving, British politicians briefed to monitor EU laws said on Tuesday.
The British government must not be railroaded as the pace of negotiations between EU members hot up over the next few months, the UK's Select Committee on European Legislation added.
"The pace of negotiations becomes much faster towards the end of an inter-governmental conference. This IGC will be no exception," a report from the committee said.
It said in the weeks and even days before the Amsterdam European council in June, the shape of the new treaty may well change significantly.

"National parliaments will have to approve the treaty. The heads of state and government will be well advised to ensure that the document which they sign in Amsterdam takes full account of the rights and expectations of parliaments." The EU's Inter-Governmental Conference is due to be completed in Amsterdam with an updated treaty signed by mid-June, shortly before the Netherlands' stint with the EU presidency ends.
The Select Committee, comprising both Eurosceptic and Europhile members of parliament, agreed national parliaments had a crucial role to play in the EU far into the future.

"However the European Union develops, not just as a result of the Treaty which is to be concluded in June but far into the 21st century, national parliaments will play a unique and vital role," it said.

"Scale and distance will always mean national parliaments are the primary focus of democratic legitimacy in the union. They are closer to the citizen, and have a special part to play in providing the responsiveness and control the Union needs."
The committee said all national parliaments tied in to the EU should have texts of European proposals in time for careful analysis, debate and influence before decisions are taken.
A draft protocol on the role of parliaments, put together at the EU's Dublin summit, basically said the same thing.

The British MPs broadly welcomed the protocol but said it did not go far enough. "We must point out that, as presently drafted, it falls some way short of our recommendations and the UK government's formal proposal."
The protocol should be widened to apply the minimum notice period to pre-legislative documents and broadened beyond just the interests of parliaments, the committee said.
"The protocol must give those who will be affected by legislation time to see it in draft and have an input into the process, whether throught their national parliaments or otherwise."
